Our objective is to initiate a comprehensive binary catalog from the LAMOST time-domain survey (LTS) data. To achieve this, we first analyzed the LTS data reduction pipeline and developed an optimized algorithm to detect binary candidates. Subsequently, we compiled a catalog containing binary candidates from the LTS data spanning one year (2018-2019), incorporating 1,065,556 candidates and confirmed resolvable binaries amounting to 1,004 in number. Additionally, we carried out a thorough assessment of our detection algorithm and formulated recommendations for enhancing its accuracy.

The role of a true random number generator (TRNG) is crucial in numerous applications, requiring continuous supply of high-quality random numbers. Existing TRNG designs face challenges in meeting performance demands, with trade-offs between co-processors, throughput, and energy consumption. The C++ library, CTR, facilitates the development of platform-agnostic TRNGs by leveraging diverse hardware platforms, yet its reliance on multiple instruction set architectures (ISAs) hinders its performance, particularly in terms of throughput and energy efficiency. The c++ based TRNG, TuRaN TRNG, overcomes these limitations by utilizing a single ISA, enabling seamless compilation across various hardware platforms. The proposed design enhances randomness by combining a primary entropy source with a conditional feedback mechanism, thereby ensuring high-quality output. The integration of these elements results in significant improvements, with TuRaN TRNG achieving 10.5x higher throughput and 2.5x lower energy consumption compared to leading commercial and research-based TRNGs.

A specific type of electrochemical capacitor, specifically a single-electron transistor made from carbon nanotubes, exhibits unique resistive switching behavior. When this effect is observed, the resulting switch exhibits an unusually high ratio of on to off currents, significantly higher than typical single-electron devices. Notably, the memory cells based on this switch offer excellent scalability, potentially reaching a size 1000 times smaller than conventional DRAM at just 10 nanometers in dimension. What's more, the memory cells demonstrate exceptional endurance, capable of withstanding up to $10^{14}$ cycles, and also show signs of excellent data retention, even after being subjected to extreme temperature fluctuations.

The application of a modern understanding of the causal representation of Feynman integrands has led to substantial progress in multi-loop computations, and we now provide an in-depth examination of the canonical canonical form associated with specific geometric structures. This analysis is centered around multi-loop topology and features a detailed exploration of one-loop graphs and the planar part of two-loop graphs. Our discussion is supported by an explicit consideration of the maximal Eulerian subforests in these cases.

This paper investigates the spectral properties of quantum walks using the time-evolution operator's quantum dynamical measures and Green functions. We specifically examine the discrete spatial Fourier transform of the Green functions, leveraging their asymptotic behavior and moments to derive crucial characteristics. These functions are then utilized to identify and analyze the essential spectrum, incorporating, extending, and contrasting prior research on discrete-space quantum walks.

Using recent observational data from VIRGO and LIGO for compact binary stars,
we investigated the characteristics of hybrid stars containing quark cores, modeled
after the MRFOD and RMF frameworks, and incorporated a bag constant, spin-zero,
and spin-one vector terms. We analyzed the mass-radius relationships of hybrid stars
in relation to the mass of a given neutron star, the amount of deconfined quark,
and various model constants, and also mapped out the stability limits for each model.
We established that hybrid stars can have masses up to twice the neutron star mass,
with masses up to 2.68 and 2.72 times the mass of the sun for the MRFOD and RMF
models, respectively. We found an increase in radius as quark deconfinement increased,
and that both models can match real-world data when accounting for a specific quark
mass, but the MRFOD model offers the best likelihood for a mass of 2.01 times the
mass of the sun.

We examine an optomechanical system that integrates a $q$-deformed two-level atom, an optical cavity, and a movable mirror. The system includes an incoming probe field, a intracavity field, and an optomechanical interaction, with coupling between the intracavity field and the target level of the two-level atom. By adjusting tunneling strength and optomechanical coupling, the model can support normal and anomalous transmission effects. Further analysis shows that tunneling and coupling parameters influence the q-deformation parameter, leading to changes in the transmitted probe field. The study of steady-state populations, including both normal and anomalous orderings, along with the mean mechanical response, is also conducted. The system's ability to generate non-Gaussian states in the mean mechanical response is found to depend on tunneling and coupling parameters.

This study focuses on the scissors mode, a specific excitation mode found in certain groups of atoms, specifically even-odd, odd-even, and odd-odd nuclei near a major energy shell, using both theoretical calculations and experimental data. Research has identified two distinct types of this excitation, known as R-positive and R-negative, distinguished by their different magnetic transition properties. Calculations using a specific model have shown that certain nuclei exhibit a significant R-negative mode, with a specific transition property value, whereas others display primarily R-positive modes with varying property values. Comparing predicted and experimental data has revealed discrepancies, with certain experimentally verified scissors modes not matching theoretical predictions. Additionally, experimental data has identified new, previously unconfirmed R-negative modes in a specific group of atoms, with a specific property value, matching predicted values.

This research examines the phenomenon of metal-to-insulator transition in graphene
and bismuth ferrite through computational modeling, focusing on how electronic
properties change based on material thickness. For graphene, a metal-insulator transition
is observed as thickness decreases to monolayer form, influenced by electronic band
structure changes and space confinement. Similarly, in bismuth ferrite, a metal-insulator
transition with hysteresis occurs with thickness reduction to monolayer, attributed to
shifts in electronic band structure and exchange interactions. These findings offer
insights into how electronic properties are affected by quantum confinement in thin films
and pave the way for the development of novel nanoscale devices utilizing ultrathin materials.

A novel statistical framework, rooted in heavy-tailed distributions, has the potential to provide insights into complex atomic and molecular behaviors governed by quantum effects. By applying tools from heavy-tailed statistics to laser-cooled atomic groups, we've discovered that these systems exhibit characteristics that can be better understood through statistical features such as infinite variance and Leptokurtosis. This approach enables the identification of emergent collective phenomena, including phase transitions and self-organization, as well as more accurate simulations of these systems. Our analysis demonstrates that the applicability of this approach is not limited to specific atomic species or experimental setups, but rather spans a broad range of conditions.

In 2021, the cryptocurrency market experienced significant volatility amid an unprecedented bull run. Our research focuses on the trading network's network characteristics, analyzed through edge- and node-based models. Our findings reveal that edge-based models exhibited heightened complexity as transaction volumes surged in the first half of 2021, whereas node-based models showed a decline in complexity. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that market transactions increasingly concentrated among a smaller group of traders over time.

A combined approach of quantum and molecular dynamics simulations, designed to investigate proton transfer between $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O}$, successfully uncovers how zero-point motion affects their molecular interaction. As a result, it's observed that the energy barrier for a specific proton transfer reaction decreases significantly, approximately 15 kJ/mol, compared to classical molecular dynamics simulations, highlighting the critical influence of zero-point motion in the $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O}$ interaction. Furthermore, the simulations reveal enhanced stability in the $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O}$ molecular complex due to the enhanced proton transfer, providing evidence of the significant impact of zero-point motion on the molecular interaction between these substances.

Consider a set of operators that are both non-expansive and invariant to a specific group's transformations. If the underlying spaces are sufficiently large, these operators can be perfectly represented in a set of compact, fully expansive functions, even if the functions belong to different metric spaces. The proof of this concept involves showing that the original set of operators can be mapped to a set of its maximal expansive functions, which can then be shown to contain smaller copies of the original set. Additionally, some research questions are explored, including the evaluation of several specific embedding scenarios.

A study is conducted to determine whether the Einstein relation holds in systems with spatially varying temperature profiles. This investigation involves simulating colloidal particles in a solvent with different constant temperature settings, creating temperature gradients that cannot be controlled at the system boundaries. The diffusion coefficients and mobility of the particles are measured in these conditions, and it is found that the Einstein relation does not hold above low Fokker-Planck characteristic activity levels, implying non-equilibrium diffusion. Further analysis reveals an approximate equivalence between the effective diffusion coefficient and the equilibrium diffusion coefficient calculated using the local thermodynamic free energy, although this does not fully account for all corrections.

In many applications, deep learning models are required to establish a balance between underfitting and overfitting, which often involves the application of training rules, such as parameter norm regularization, to simplify model structures.  Research into the effect of these rules on model simplicity, however, is frequently conducted using theoretical models that are not representative of real-world data, raising doubts about the generalizability of the findings.  This study aims to shed light on this issue by investigating whether stochastic gradient descent with momentum and weight decay simplify deep learning models in real-world scenarios, and if so, whether the resulting models can be attributed to the application of these rules or another mechanism, such as data availability.  To this end, we analyze the impact of four different training conditions - the absence of regularization and momentum, the presence of weight decay alone, momentum alone, and the combined effect of both - on the performance of a ResNet-50 model trained on various subsets of the ImageNet data.  The results indicate that both momentum and weight decay contribute to the over-regularization of deep learning models, which can lead to significant differences in model performance, particularly when the available training data is limited.  These findings highlight the importance of considering the interplay between different training rules and data availability when designing training protocols for deep learning models, particularly in scenarios where the available training data is scarce.

A maximum likelihood fit is commonly used in LHCb analysis to derive physical parameters, and an unbinned approach generally offers better precision while being more computationally intensive. We have developed an algorithm that significantly speeds up this process by specifically taking advantage of the $B^0 \leftrightarrow \overline{B^0}$ oscillation, which is unique to the LHCb detector's setup due to its forward design. By doing so, we can eliminate the need for one dimension in phase space, reduce processing to half, and take full advantage of the detector's capabilities. The improved speed allows for more thorough exploration of parameter space, a feature particularly valuable in beyond-the-Standard-Model searches that demand a high degree of flexibility. When applied to $B^0 \to K^0_{\mathrm{short}}$ decays from the DILU dataset, tests showed that our unbinned algorithm matches the accuracy of its binned counterpart, but when used on $B^0_d \to D^0_{\mathrm{light}} \pi^{\pm}$ determinations, our results indicated an unbinned method to be approximately twice as precise.

The performance of pre-trained language models, such as BERT, in article scoring has been hindered by the small size of available datasets. To overcome this limitation, a new method is presented that leverages data augmentation and multi-task learning to enhance its performance. By applying data augmentation techniques, such as copying, shuffling, and swapping, the size of the training dataset can be increased threefold. Additionally, a data selection method is used to maintain high-quality augmented data. Furthermore, combining this augmentation with BERT's pre-trained knowledge through multi-task learning allows the model to learn from diverse training examples more effectively. As a result, the proposed method significantly outperforms both fine-tuning BERT and its variant without pre-training on two datasets.

We examine statistical techniques for determining continuous parameters in theoretical models based on conditional independence relationships. Two specific examples of such models are considered: a Bayesian network parameterized by a Poisson distribution and a Gaussian graphical model. We examine the feasibility of consistent parameter estimation in these models from the statistical perspective, and when possible, we propose and evaluate methods that achieve this. Our analysis of the GG model includes the development of estimators that combine discrete vertex observations with real-valued data to estimate the precision matrix, which can be done efficiently in a statistically adequate manner. We demonstrate that standard optimization-based approaches fail in this context, and instead provide and evaluate an alternative approach based on discrete observations discretized using a suitable cutoff value.

The distribution of societal opportunities is an equitable concern, and although the allocation aims to enhance people's lives in the present, it often ends up exacerbating socio-economic disparities for subsequent generations. This phenomenon is referred to as the Paradox of Equity. By employing a simple model of opportunity allocation in an infinite horizon setting, we demonstrate that strict equality can worsen the socioeconomic status of the population over time. Conversely, we show that prioritizing less advantaged individuals, rather than equal distribution, can mitigate this paradox.

This study investigates the sign factor that arises when the wavefunctions of identical particles are permuted, linking it to the particles' spin value, as per the spin-statistics theorem. The permutation operation is represented using a discrete unitary symmetry, and the resulting sign factor is identified as either +1 or -1. The spin value of a particle determines the sign factor, with even spin resulting in +1 and odd spin in -1. The theory is then extended to account for fractional spin particles, giving rise to anyonic behavior.

Cryptocurrency, particularly Monero, offers robust security through encryption, but its transaction verification process is time-consuming, making large transactions impractical to include in a single block. To address this, our proposed solution, Delegated RingCT, enables a verifier to efficiently confirm a batch of transactions at a constant time, thereby increasing block capacity. By allowing verifiers to outsource task-intensive decryption to trusted servers, Delegated RingCT significantly speeds up verification at the cost of some level of trust. We further extend this concept to handle rings of varying sizes, providing flexibility for adaptability to different use cases.

We investigate the complexity of approximately solving systems of linear equations, focusing on the class lases. Our research establishes interconnections between various aspects such as inter-solver relationships, circuit computation models, and inter-problem relationships that define lases. Specifically, we relate lases to NP under quasi-polynomial time reductions with approximate oracle access. Additionally, inter-solver relationships can be understood through circuits, where an inter-solver relationship can be represented by a TC^0 reduction, and conversely, any TC^0 reduction can be translated into an inter-solver relationship. Similarly, we show that an inter-solver relationship can be established through a TC^0 circuit, and different variants of linear systems, such as lases and lases, demonstrate equivalence in their respective complexity.

Researchers have gathered and analyzed additional data from a 13 TeV proton-proton collision at the Large Hadron Collider, resulting in a combined luminosity of 359 inverse femtobarns. The analysis focused on the individual and combined cross-sections of WW, ZZ, and other processes in the W leptonic and electronic channels. The measured production rates for ZZ and other processes showed excellent agreement with the Standard Model predictions, exhibiting deviations of just 1.3 and 1 standard deviation respectively. The observed cross-sections of WW and other processes exhibited discrepancies of 2 and 1 standard deviation respectively. The measured cross-sections along with the predicted uncertainties demonstrated consistency with the Standard Model expectations.

We analyze the progress in UD-based NLP for Hebrew from 2017 to 2022, and demonstrate how a new UD treebank significantly boosted state-of-the-art results. We evaluated all models competing in the SemEval workshops, and found that modern approaches generally outperformed previous ones, despite competing on older datasets. Our in-depth analysis shows that a new training dataset and related tools primarily accounted for the improvement in performance.

J. Bourgain established in 1982 that any epsilon-isometric reduction of dimension by a convex body can be achieved through John's ellipsoid, which implies the existence of an epsilon-isometric dimension reduction for any convex body. This result has been expanded upon by B. Klartag, who found an epsilon-isometric body related to the original if the reduction is of high dimension, and by B. Klartag and B. Peres, who found the same outcome for reductions to any sufficiently large dimension. The outcome is true for the unit ball of a n-dimensional normed space, denoted as ell_p, except for p=2, where it is known that linear operators can achieve epsilon-isometric dimension reduction. However, it remains unknown whether such reductions can be accomplished through John's ellipsoid in this specific case.

In continuum mechanics, modeling history-dependent plasticity behavior through constitutive laws poses a challenge that is now being tackled via a novel approach. The proposed method leverages unbounded continual learning in combination with kernel-based neural networks to create a plasticity model that can adapt to different materials in real-time as new data becomes available, all the while maintaining accuracy and avoiding data overviews through a careful adjustment of the learning process.

Theoretical research on LDPC codes was conducted, with a focus on the LDPC code ensembles defined by the probability distribution of their check node degrees. The theoretical probability distribution of the check node degree was derived, and its impact on the maximum tolerable erasure probability in the Shannon LDPC code ensemble was examined. It was found that including degrees with lower values than the average degree significantly reduces the maximum tolerable erasure probability, and the performance gap can be as large as 10% when the fraction of such degrees increases from 0 to 0.5, with the fraction held constant at 0 near the capacity threshold. Notably, an increase in the average edge degree results in a decrease in the negative degree-to-degree correlation, and the decrease in this correlation corresponds to an increase in the maximum tolerable erasure probability, particularly for higher average edge degrees (greater than 4).

This paper proposes the Optimal Multi-step Predictive Safe Forming Control (OMPSFC) as a model predictive control method for controlling complex systems with uncertain dynamics under various constraints. A forming model is designed in the presence of bounded disturbances, with safety assurances for linear systems and extended differentiability for nonlinear systems. A time-varying cost function is optimized in the OMPSFC, taking into account past inputs and states to determine an optimal future trajectory. Numerical examples demonstrate the effectiveness of the OMPSFC in optimizing performance while maintaining robustness and constraint satisfaction.

In a study of 23,210 multilingual models, researchers investigated whether there's a connection between how well models perform on few-shot in-context learning tasks and their language modeling performance. They analyzed these models across 51 different languages and found that, although improvements in few-shot in-context learning performance don't necessarily lead to comparable improvements in language modeling, there's a consistent relationship between the two, regardless of language. Specifically, models with higher language modeling accuracy tend to have better few-shot in-context learning performance. However, this finding is complicated by the presence of outliers, which led to the development of outlier-detection techniques for identifying exceptional models. Once these outliers were removed, outliers' removal significantly clarified the previously observed correlations.

We've examined the impact of anisotropic thermal conductivity on galaxy clusters with high temperatures, using data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. Our analysis reveals that colder air within clusters can grow approximately 1.5 to 2 times faster when heat conducts more efficiently along the direction of the cluster's main axis, as opposed to uniform heat conductivity. Furthermore, simulations indicate that this air contraction can become even more pronounced - potentially enhancing contraction rates by an additional 50 percent - in clusters where the ratio of vertical to horizontal conductivity is 2.5 or greater.

The Standard Model of particle physics faces challenges in addressing the matter-antimatter imbalance, which is essential for the existence of matter. This issue, known as the CP asymmetry problem, has been a central concern in research for several decades. As researchers have developed more sensitive tools, they have been able to study the properties of various particles in greater detail. The advancements in technology have allowed for the direct study of various particles, including beauty baryons, charm mesons, and charmed baryons. Recent findings on CP asymmetry in these particles have provided some insight, but the solution to the broader issue remains unclear. This review focuses on CP asymmetry in beauty baryons and related topics, offering a comprehensive examination of current experimental findings and theoretical analysis.

Our new findings regarding hard string scattering amplitudes show good agreement with prior conjectures concerning the energy transformation rules in string theory, but the calculated ratios do not precisely match the proposed rules, especially not at the limit, and suggest a differing behavior when scattered beyond the string scale, which contradicts the concept of string duality symmetry at high energies.

This study addresses the problem of optimizing workloads across a cluster of edge computing nodes to minimize power consumption. The objective is to reduce the total energy used by workloads processed at the edge, while ensuring that no individual edge facility exceeds its maximum power capacity. Given the complexity and intractability of the problem, we propose a simplified model and an efficient dynamic programming solution. The optimization strategy involves workloads being assigned to edge computing nodes, which then process them either locally or by offloading to the cloud, based on age constraints. The feasibility of the optimization is evaluated through cloud storage requirements, processing times, and data transfer costs. To address various generalizations, we also develop suitable solution approaches. The results of computational experiments confirm the effectiveness of our approach and its ability to significantly reduce energy consumption at edge computing facilities, without incurring any negative impact on the cloud facility's energy usage.

Language models in speech synthesis generate sequences of latent states, comprising transients and steady states. Analysis reveals that the speech segments corresponding to these states cluster based on their source text. Training the model to produce clusters of latent states improves its performance, as demonstrated by experiments showing comparable quality but more compact clusters. This, in turn, allows for efficient inference by reducing the size of the generative model.

This work presents a novel, practical method for optimizing the movement of robots with multiple limbs in complex environments, addressing the challenge posed by high computation costs associated with stage-by-stage optimization. We enhance efficiency by reducing problem dimensions, merging stages where feasible, and leveraging distributed computing resources to accelerate resolution. Our optimized approach is validated through real-world experiments on a tricycle robot, demonstrating reduced computation times in practice.

In various applications, it is essential to obtain a reliable quantum system, and to achieve this, the concept of state distillation has been developed, which involves converting multiple weakly-resourceful states into a single highly-resourceful state, ideally a maximally-resourceful pure state, known as the standard form.  Two distinct approaches to distillation, one focusing on exact attainment of the standard form and the other allowing for some error tolerance, are explored, and their trade-offs are characterized.  While the approach to exact attainment prioritizes minimizing the number of copies needed, the approach allowing for some error tolerance focuses on minimizing the failure probability, and these two objectives lead to different optimization problems.  By investigating these problems, it is found that they can be reformulated as various optimization problems under specific constraints, and characterizing the relevant constraints leads to a more comprehensive understanding of the theoretical limitations of distillation.  The solutions provided are general, applicable to any set of states and any quantum resource theory, and the outcomes are expressed as solutions to specific optimization problems under specific constraints, which in turn provide novel characterizations of the applicable regions in question.

The behavior of a coffee cup in transition between standing and sitting positions varies greatly depending on the location of the pivot point, which presents an intriguing opportunity for a dynamic demonstration of the effects of acceleration and refraction of light. A stable method to pour coffee from a moving container can be achieved by predicting and correcting for changes caused by dynamics, and by utilizing the simpler principle that relies only on the refraction of light, which can be CHIMED by changing the container's speed and direction.

We investigate the performance of stochastic gradient descent with momentum, with and without clipping, in decentralized learning across a network of multiple devices. Analyzing a $\mu$-strongly monotone problem, with gradients that have a Lipschitz continuity property, we compare the behavior with and without gradient clipping. Our analysis of the decentralized learning algorithm with gradient clipping in the stochastic setting yields convergence, at a rate of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu T}}$ after $T$ iterations, at a distance of $\frac{\sqrt{L^2 + G^2}}{\sqrt{e^{\frac{2\mu}{L}} - 1}\sqrt{N}\mu T}$ from the optimal solution. Our results, which confirm the effectiveness of gradient clipping, also provide an exponential upper bound of $\frac{L}{\mu}e^{\frac{2\mu}{L}}$ on the condition number of the objective function in the decentralized setting, thereby improving previous results, particularly those of [A. Lyuliang et al., 2020], and demonstrating that clipping enables faster convergence, at a rate of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}T}$, for large enough Lipschitz constants.

The rapidity and $p_{\rm t}$ yields of charged particles in nucleus-nucleus collisions are examined across a range of collisions, from small systems to the LHC, incorporating the impact of pre-equilibrium entropy generation and particle creation. Our results demonstrate that a consistent framework can explain the complete set of data, encompassing flow, with the requirement that the final system's entropy is significantly larger than its initial state.

A theoretical model of early star formation has been developed, incorporating the dynamics of mass ejection and mass loss in a three-dimensional, time-dependent framework. The model simulates the collapse of a uniform spherical cloud, triggered by a decrease in pressure, and features a uniform magnetic field aligned with the vertical axis. The numerical approach utilized in this work has not previously been published in scientific literature, and it has now been applied to various scenarios in order to understand how mass ejection and mass loss influence the process of star formation. The results demonstrate that mass ejection can occur in two distinct phases, with the first phase characterized by significant mass loss and the second phase marked by rapid accretion. The first phase of ejection can be further divided into sub-phases, with the first sub-phase characterized by strong mass loss and the second sub-phase marked by weaker mass loss. The amount of mass lost in the first phase is strongly influenced by the cloud's mass and the strength of the magnetic field, whereas the amount of mass lost in the second phase is negligible. The findings of this work suggest that mass ejection can have a substantial impact on the process of star formation, and that the amount of mass lost in the early phases can be as much as 50% of the initial cloud mass.

In line with B. F. Skyrms's yoke theory, which maintains that systems' inherent order arises from their response to destabilizing factors, our research proposes a Yoke Compensating Architecture (YCA) for cyber-physical systems. The YCA is an effective framework for maintaining safety in systems, as exemplified in its application to the classic pendulum problem. In order to account for complex, non-linear system behaviors, we utilize a specialized feedback control mechanism and an adaptive autoencoder to identify compensating features within raw data. The results demonstrate that YCA is a viable solution for maintaining high levels of safety and sustaining complex system orders, particularly in systems subject to random disturbances.

This study investigates the range of possible orbital distortions an uncontrollable object can experience due to interactions with solar radiation pressure lobe resonances, given various types of oblateness resonances, such as those found in moonlets, planets, and comets. To accomplish this, the research utilizes two different methods: one involving detailed numerical simulations and another using a simplified analytical approach. The findings reveal significant disparities in the predicted ranges of eccentricity and inclination variations, highlighting the need for more precise and reliable prediction tools in the field of debris management.

To enhance the velocity gauge's (VG) description of electromagnetic (EM) interactions within the linear response domain, its shortcoming is attributed to an inaccurate electron Hamiltonian description. By applying a gauge-invariant (G) transformation, the voltage gauge (VG) Hamiltonian is revised, yielding the improved G voltage gauge (VGG) model. Notably, VGG incorporates a scalar G-transformed electron potential and modified vector potential, accounting for the influence of lattice periodicity. Analytical and numerical evaluations demonstrate that VGG not only recovers key aspects of electron dynamics observed in first principles simulations, but also accurately describes EM field influence on electron band structure, adiabatic entanglement, and back-stress force on bands, outperforming existing models in various regimes.

The traditional EM algorithm is widely used for estimating the parameters of a 3D object from a single image, combining direct and iterative methods to handle measurement errors and unknown information. However, it often gets trapped in local solutions and is sensitive to outliers, making it unreliable in certain cases. In this research, we develop a more robust version of the algorithm by creating a graph where 3D model points are nodes and the connections represent the relationships between them. By separating the estimation of the object's pose, shape, and size into separate steps on this graph, we introduce a new method to estimate the object more reliably. This method takes advantage of recent progress in direct estimation, resulting in faster computations. To further improve the robustness of the estimator, we use a weighted version of the estimator that can be optimized more efficiently. In numerical tests, we show that the graph-theoretic approach and the conditional M-step lead to better results, especially in the presence of outliers.

We examine the confidence regions for one- and two-dimensional parameter spaces in the cauchy distribution using the l-infinity and l-1 norms in their geometric representations. These regions are found to be relatively straightforward to explain visually, particularly when considering the l-1 based approach. This method initially involves an arbitrary choice, but can subsequently refine that choice in a way that necessitates fewer computations and produces a less conservative estimate, resulting in a more practical approximation that yields one-dimensional confidence intervals that are easier to interpret. A simulation study is used to compare the performance of various methods for estimating cauchy distribution parameters and shows that methods based on the l-1 confidence intervals often fail to control type 1 error rates, whereas our two-stage procedure successfully maintains the desired error control.

In clinical trials with multiple treatments, data from trials that have already been completed can be utilized to enhance the efficiency of the ongoing trials. This can be achieved by incorporating information from similar trials that have been conducted using a comparable randomization scheme. For instance, a borrowing approach can be implemented by adjusting the initial sample size or by modifying the treatment assignments during the trial. Although these methods have been implemented using simulated data, their effectiveness has yet to be evaluated using real-world data. Therefore, a real-data analysis was performed to assess their relative efficiencies when applied to the analysis of pediatric trials that are part of the Pediatric Oncology Group's four-phase adaptive randomization trials. A total of 139 trials were analyzed, of which 69 were randomly controlled and 70 were controlled using the adaptive randomization scheme. The results revealed that adaptive randomization schemes can reduce the sample size by up to 30% while still maintaining similar statistical power. Furthermore, the analysis found that the efficiency of borrowing depends on the degree of commensurability between the trials being analyzed. The findings suggest that borrowing can be effectively utilized to reduce sample sizes without compromising statistical power.

This study investigates how variable dynamics based on position impact the tracking performance of motion control systems, a common feature in common applications like robot manipulation and vehicle navigation. To investigate the subject, a nonlinear control method is proposed that utilizes velocity feedback and a compensating term to account for the variable dynamics in system control, along with a real-time estimation of unmeasurable acceleration. This strategy ensures bounded performance without requiring precise knowledge of dynamics variables, a requirement in prior research methods. The new design does not require partitioning the working area into specific regions, a common requirement in prior research methods.

We developed an object classification framework that leverages learned object alignment representations from a novel, unsupervised deep learning network for point cloud registration. The network aligns 3D object views without prior knowledge, using a novel loss function that promotes object alignment based on local geometric features. The resulting object alignment embeddings are found to be particularly effective in both 3D and 2D-3D object classification tasks, achieving top-notch performance with minimal or no additional training.

The d-$R_	ext{all}$-nilpotency degree is defined as a characteristic of (r, s) -groups, which helps to categorize these groups based on their nilpotency degree relative to arbitrary subgroups. In part, an $R_	ext{all}$-nilpotent group is an (r, 1)-group, and it has been established that a d-r,1 -group exists for every odd integer r, whereas d-r,2 -groups do not exist for r > 2. Furthermore, it has been proven that a certain class of (r, 2)-groups, which are d-r,2 -groups, have an abelian factor group, and it has been established that the nilpotency degree of this class is 3.

A precise determination of the standard model parameters, including $m_t$, is highly desirable. Even a modest electron-positron collider or a smaller muon collider can accurately measure $m_t$ through threshold resummation techniques in muon-muon collisions, enabling comparisons with other production methods. Additionally, a smaller muon collider demonstrator can make significant contributions to determining $m_t$ by utilizing two distinct techniques: reconstructing $m_t$ from fully decayed top quarks produced in muon-muon collisions and employing mass taggers for fully decayed standard model $Z$-bosons produced in muon-muon collisions, providing information about $m_t$ via off-shell $Z$-bosons in fully decayed top quark pairs.

We've developed an innovative method to reconstruct the initial conditions of time-resolved spectroscopy experiments, which is particularly useful for studying chemical and physical processes that evolve over time. This method overcomes the limitation of conventional linear approaches, which are sensitive to experimental noise, by accurately inquiring about non-linear interactions between light and matter. Furthermore, we've implemented a efficient Monte Carlo algorithm that speeds up the reconstruction process and allows for the analysis of large datasets. The accuracy of our method is validated through simulations of various types of experiments, including those involving isolated molecules and scattering events, as well as cluster ionization and relaxation. The method is also applied to a real-world experiment, which studied the ultra-fast dynamics of electron emission in thin metal films. The results demonstrate that our method is capable of accurately extracting initial conditions even from noisy data, which is a significant improvement over previous methods.

We examine the q-qbar-q distribution amplitudes for $S$-wave $ud$-type vector mesons ($\rho$, $\rho^*$) and $D^*$ mesons ($D^*_0$, $D^*_1$, $D^*_2$), as well as the distribution amplitudes for $ud$-type pseudoscalar ($\pi$) and ($\eta_\pi$). Using a quark model based on light-cone gauge wave functions derived from ground-state light-cone wave functions, we find that the three quark density is symmetric under quark exchange for most of these states, except for $D^*_0$ and $D^*_2$ which exhibit non-trivial $q^2$ behavior. Furthermore, the correlation between quark and diquark momenta in vector ($\pi$) and ($\rho$) shows a direct proportionality with a coefficient of approximately 2, as expected from their comparable masses. However, in the heavy-meson $D^*$ system, this relationship deviates due to the influence of the c-quark mass.

This study delves into the growth estimates of modified Fourier transforms, considering functions within Gelfand-Shilov spaces and connected to holomorphic functions, as well as generalized harmonic polybernomials. We also explore potential applications in addressing the problem of extending harmonic polynomials.

This study introduces CySGAN, a conditional GAN-based method for producing a vast number of varied object images, which significantly boosts the accuracy of object image instance segmentation. Existing image instance segmentation methods face a major challenge in obtaining large, diverse training datasets. The proposed CySGAN method overcomes this limitation by generating large numbers of varied object images in a single step, which in turn leads to a substantial 10% increase in the mean pixel-based accuracy of object image instance segmentation. The approach has been extensively tested on the COCO dataset, with the most impressive result being the use of a Mask R-CNN backbone and a YOLOv3 detector, where CySGAN achieved a 9.76% increase in mean pixel-based accuracy over the existing real data approach.

Deep neural networks capable of anticipating next actions are crucial for enabling robots to adapt to varying levels of human interaction. Despite significant progress using deep neural networks, architectures based on recurrent connections are hindered by their slow convergence and sensitivity to inputs. Recent advancements in compositional model design have highlighted the effectiveness of integrating modular structures over fully connected networks. Building on this research, our study introduces a novel module tailored for action anticipation models consisting of deep neural networks processing sequential data. This modular design targets the specific challenges inherent to these tasks and enhances overall performance. Specifically, our research demonstrates the following contributions: (1) the development of a new module for action anticipation models; (2) evidence of its effectiveness in improving existing models' accuracy, especially with limited training data; and (3) the incorporation of an additional module utilizing Radial Basis Function kernels for temporal signal interpretation; and (4) demonstration of its practical value through applications in action anticipation models.

Recent observations of the star Proxima Centauri in the X-ray band have provided new insights into the temporal and wavelength-dependent behavior of its flares. A high-resolution spectrograph observed the star, and the data were used to determine the properties of the star's flares across multiple spectral ranges. The study found that the star's flares exhibit a clear correlation between the broadening of certain hydrogen spectral lines and the star's overall spectral energy distribution. The relationship observed suggests that the star's flares exhibit a characteristic two-power law spectrum, and that the broadening of certain hydrogen lines is caused by the presence of a localized, high-velocity plasma during the flares. The study also found that the star's flares exhibit a distinct velocity pattern, and that the star's overall spectral energy distribution exhibits a complex structure, and that the star's overall spectral energy distribution exhibits a complex structure, and that the star's overall spectral energy distribution exhibits a complex structure.

We have developed an explicit expression for the first-order deformation operator of G2-instantons on manifolds with a G2 structure. Using this expression, we can assess the rigidity of these instantons. The expression also enables us to decompose G2-instantons on product 3-manifolds into their constituent parts. This allows us to classify certain classified g2-instantons up to isomorphism and examine the freedom of gauge symmetry in these classifications. Furthermore, we have studied the rigidity of abelian instantons within the group of such symmetries.

To establish the normality of operators, we employ the concept of commutant variable, initially introduced as the first non-trivial point spectrum of the difference operator. We determine all the point spectra of the difference operator $D$, and subsequently identify, through confluence of Conjugate, Weight, and Projection cases, the conditions under which composition and weighted composition operators are normal.

We've established a key connection between specific partitions of the form $(\lambda, 0)$, where $\lambda$ consists only of prime power components, and the concept of largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions. To achieve this, we drew on the work of Brinon and Kl\"{u}ners in developing a theory of largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions, which relies heavily on the principles of modular arithmetic. Furthermore, we introduced a theory of key $p$-core $p'$-partitions, which also yields notable results. Our analysis also shows that both the theory of largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions and key $p$-core $p'$-partitions can be modeled using a specific combinatorial structure known as abacus theory in characteristic $p$.

Three-dimensional point cloud models are gaining traction in a variety of fields, but their vulnerability to malicious attacks is a pressing concern. In this research, we introduce the Training-Perturbation-Collision (TPC) framework, which enhances the robustness of 3D point cloud models against a specific type of attack known as object rotation. Our TPC approach consists of two main components: a procedure to generate and refine attack samples with high efficiency, and a corresponding training mechanism that allows the defender to counter these transformations with superior accuracy and security. Experiments on three widely used datasets demonstrate the practical value of the TPC framework, showing a notable improvement in certified accuracy against this specific type of attack, while maintaining similar performance against other common attacks and preserving similar model accuracy.

This research outlines a simulation framework for analyzing Free-Space Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar systems, enabling the modeling and performance assessment of individual radar networks or multi-radar setups following ALOHA-based scheduling protocols. By incorporating various factors such as chirp configuration, target presence, and environmental environment, this framework allows for calculating interference probabilities, target detection likelihoods, and system throughput. Key findings demonstrate that interference probabilities and system throughput are significantly influenced by the number of chirps per packet utilized, while it is found that a greater number of packets per second yields higher detection rates but also higher interference rates.

A theoretical model is developed to quantify the detection of two-photon absorption of entangled photons in solid materials by adapting the Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility of an interferogram as a metric. The visibility of the Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram is found to be directly influenced by the degree of two-photon absorption, enabling its use as a detection tool. The model examines the visibility of the Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram in the context of two-photon absorption in solid materials and the effects of detection inefficiencies on its visibility. It is shown that while efficient detectors maintain high visibility, the visibility is diminished by detection inefficiencies. An optimal balance between efficiency and the visibility of the Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram visibility is identified in terms of inflection points. The model's predictions are validated experimentally with the observation that while detecting absorption with less than 50% efficient detectors is possible, accurate measurement of absorption requires detectors with no errors.

Let $T$ be a torus that acts freely on an elliptic curve $E$. Our goal is to establish that the $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology of $E$, denoted as $\Ell_{\Ell_T}(E)$, within the context of 2-periodic elliptic spectra, is isomorphic to the ordinary elliptic cohomology of a specific lens space, also defined period 2.

This work addresses the challenge of filling in temporal knowledge graphs by proposing an approach that incorporates cyclic patterns and contextual information from related entities. The method employs a novel cyclic pattern-aware time-encoding scheme that utilizes cosine functions to represent time, and an entity-dependent attention mechanism that aggregates the contextual patterns of related entities to enhance prediction accuracy. The technique's performance is evaluated using standard benchmarks, and it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of precision.

When an object collides with a solid surface, the generated sound waves can propagate through the material, reaching the microphone's position, where they are recorded as "ground sound." Although this phenomenon has been observed for some time, its exact mechanisms and applications remain underexplored. In this study, we focus on detecting ground sound and analyzing its characteristics in diverse scenarios. We find that ground sound becomes audible when projectiles such as steel balls and pellets impact surfaces, and also when smaller objects like seeds hit the ground. In contrast, when slugs crawl over a surface, the resulting ground sound is inaudible. Through numerical simulations, we determined that microphones positioned close to the impact point capture significant airborne sound, whereas those placed directly above the impact point capture predominantly ground sound. As a result, we developed an algorithm to filter out airborne sound, and successfully isolated the characteristics of ground sound, including its distinct decay pattern, frequency spectrum, and the presence of specific frequency bands. Notably, we observed that ground sound exhibits a unique "dip" around 4 kHz, and this characteristic can be utilized to differentiate it from airborne sound automatically.

In practical quantum technology settings, achieving flawless, trusted measurement devices is challenging. Consequently, we examined scenarios involving less-than-perfectly correlated trusted devices, which have significant implications for Bell nonlocality in applied quantum information technology. We found that even modest levels of correlation can yield nonlocal correlations that surpass a randomly generated pool's capabilities in various tasks, particularly in technology settings where a single copy of shared randomness is often more practical than multiple copies required for perfect correlation distribution. We demonstrated that reliable extraction of nearly perfect correlations from imperfectly shared randomness and vice versa is possible even when correlations are locally determined, regardless of the number of parties involved. Finally, we applied our results to the field of device-based randomness expansion and found that reliable extraction of perfect correlations from imperfectly correlated locally determined variables can be accomplished through the technology of hash functions.

In materials science, flat bands are a significant phenomenon, yet they are often difficult to identify.  We have developed a method to find and characterize degenerate flat bands in systems of any dimensionality, combining topology, computational modeling, and statistical analysis.  Our approach involves quantifying topological features through the computation of random matrix wavefunctions and applying our precise, data-driven criteria to confirm degeneracy.  This method is demonstrated through the examination of the square honeycomb lattice and may be applied to a wide range of systems to explore the likelihood of finding degenerate flat bands in unknown materials.

Research on two-dimensional materials, particularly electron and phonon interactions within electron-phonon coupling systems, has gained significant attention in recent years. The electron-phonon coupling properties of various 2D compounds, such as transition metal dichalcogenides and graphene, have been extensively studied. In contrast, the phonon spectrum of hydrogen boride monolayers (borophene-like HBM and tungsten-based WTBM) remains largely unexplored. Our research utilizes density functional theory to investigate the phonon spectra of these monolayers. Our findings demonstrate that the inclusion of hydrogen in WTBM significantly alters its phonon properties, resulting in higher phonon frequencies and increased electron-phonon coupling compared to pure graphene. Furthermore, our results show that hydrogen phonons contribute substantially to the scattering resistance in WTBM, a property unobserved in borophene-like HBM.

Research on one-dimensional cellular automata has revealed significant connections to combinatorial patterns. Specifically, certain key properties of the cell values have been identified and demonstrated. It was observed how the distribution of certain integers within the sequence follows a specific frequency, and it was shown how the largest occurrences within the sequence adhere to a particular asymptotic distribution. Furthermore, the researchers identified how the frequency of certain integer occurrences within the sequence adheres to a specific distribution. Building upon these findings, certain novel properties of the sequence were discovered and certain previously unknown characteristics of the frequency of certain integer occurrences within the sequence were proven.

We investigate the behavior of Lie groups and finitely generated non-abelian, virtually nilpotent groups under affine transformations on their space of characters, which we find significantly differs from the behavior observed in dynam systems on tori. We establish that for groups satisfying certain conditions, there exists a continuous distribution of orbits across the space of characters, as well as dense periodic orbits. However, these properties are not guaranteed for all groups, as we demonstrate with counterexamples involving the Baum-Slikg groups, as well as potential dense periodic orbits examples for growth types of (1,2) and (2,3). We also examine the implications of these findings on the Gelfand growth type of the group.

The evaluation of automated driving systems is a crucial process, and formal methods like model checking can significantly enhance this process. By integrating multiple safety and performance goals, models of automotive systems can be developed. The complex nature of these models, which combine continuous and discrete dynamics, poses a challenge. However, using specialized models such as HyPer, which are designed for formal analysis, allows researchers to catch errors in model definitions during development. The process of model creation is illustrated through case studies of an automotive driving assistance system, allowing for comparisons and assessments of different model configurations.

The Koopman operator offers a unified approach to analyzing nonlinear systems across various domains, including control theory and data science. This work extends co-kernel operator theory to a broader context of generalized koepienoe framework. Specific generalizations of the koepienoe framework are explored in detail.

Early 18th-century scholars, including Samuel Clarke, Nicolas Fatio de Duillier, and Johann Bernoulli, disputed the meaning of Leibniz's renowned maxim, "all that is contingent has its beginning in a certain determinate concept of infinite." Some early interpreters thought Leibniz distinguished between two concepts of infinite, one bounded and one unbounded. However, recent research has shown that this view misrepresents Leibniz's own views. Clarke, Fatio, and Bernoulli accurately grasped the maxim's significance, but used it inaccurately to attack Leibniz's philosophy, often citing cases that clearly have a concept of infinite - typically divine nature - to demonstrate that Leibniz's views on necessary and contingent perfection were in conflict.

A major challenge in analyzing Planck satellite data is foreground contamination. While sophisticated techniques have been developed to eliminate foregrounds and optimize signal extraction, there's still uncertainty about whether these methods produce unbiased cosmological parameter estimates. This study investigates foreground removal's effect on parameter accuracy and precision using realistic simulations of scientific interest. Simulations show that foreground removal can introduce significant bias and reduced precision, particularly in estimates related to reionization and gravitational waves from the early universe. These findings suggest that future experiments will need to develop even more advanced methods for foreground elimination to achieve their full potential.

Let $T$ be an operator defined on a vector space, and suppose that applying $T$ to any vector in a specific set of vectors produces a linearly independent result. The question is whether applying $T$ to a sequence of vectors, where the original sequence is square and contains repeated elements, guarantees a square and possibly repeated application results in a square matrix that is invertible.

Document-based recommendation systems utilize sequential or graph-based methods to group items into documents, enhancing recommender system performance with complex items and limited data. To address this, a new document creation strategy is proposed, leveraging proximity between items to form documents similar to popularity-based filtering systems yet more personalized. This strategy, combined with a new ranking method that considers both personalization and closeness to top recommendations, significantly improves recommendation accuracy in scenarios with complex items and data constraints. Experiments were conducted using a variety of datasets and evaluation metrics, consistently showing superior accuracy over existing methods.

This research examines the connection between conditional freeness in random matrix theory and asymptotic independence of eigenvalue distributions. We demonstrate that when a subset of unitary or Hermitian random matrices exhibits conditional freeness relative to another group, it implies asymptotic independence of their respective eigenvalue distributions. We derive a crucial condition for conditional freeness, involving a specific polynomial relationship between matrix entries. We apply this result to specific cases, including asymptotic independence of overlapping semicircle and quarter circle distributions, and frequency tables from experiments with Gaussian matrices.

This paper examines real-time monitoring of temporal specifications, incorporating timing uncertainty for more practical applications. A key contribution is the introduction of an uncertainty interval concept, enabling the accurate detection of specification violations despite timing discrepancies. It also offers two monitoring algorithm variations, one prioritizing efficiency and the other, a guaranteed level of correctness. Another notable addition is the monitoring of timing-suspension events, such as system delays or resumption, to incorporate timing uncertainty into the monitoring process.

The acquisition camera on the Very Large Telescope Interferometer plays a crucial role in detecting signals from multiple beams that are delivered by the beam combiners across a wide range of wavelengths. Although its versatility has been utilized for various purposes, its fast readout rates are primarily employed to obtain initial coarse alignments. Following a series of developments, the camera's capabilities have been leveraged to implement two essential real-time feedback systems that optimize the alignment of the four telescopes and maintain optimal alignment of the beams within the interferometer. The parameters fine-tuning these stabilization systems were meticulously calibrated to ensure minimal loss of signal intensity and to keep the alignment within the desired wavelength bandwidth of 2.0-2.3 \micron. The implementation of these precision feedback systems is critical in maximizing the efficiency of the VLT Interferometer's operations.

A data point in the plane is associated with a circular region having a specific radius, and the goal is to identify at most k centers under given capacity constraints such that the overall coverage of these domains is maximized in a way that minimizes the farthest distance from any domain to its nearest center. The problem, known as the Capacitated k-Center problem with Highway Dimension at most h, presents a challenge in that its approximation within a constant factor relative to k is classified as NP-hard. This study proposes an algorithm that achieves a logarithmic factor approximation relative to k and introduces the concept of a well-rounded center, which is defined as a domain that can be fully included in a ball with radius equal to the farthest distance from any other domain to its nearest center. The task of selecting at most k centers in a way that ensures each center is well-rounded thus becomes a distinct problem, leading to the development of a 2-approximation algorithm for this new issue with a running time dependent on n and high at most (logkh)^O(h).

In a recent study by Yang and Zhang, a particular instance of the Brück conjecture was resolved for entire functions of a non-integer order less than 1/2, involving entire functions $f$ that satisfy the equation $f(T, f) - 1^{(n)}(c) = 1^{(n)}(c)$, and having the property that the number of solutions to $f(T, f) - 1^{(n)}(c) = 1^{(n)}(c)$ is equal to the canonical divisor's number of solutions to $f(T, f) = 1^{(n)}(c) = 1^{(n)}(c)$. In this paper, a new result is presented, proving that if $f$ is a transcendental entire function, $a$ and $b$ are distinct nonzero complex numbers, and the differences $(H(T, f) - 1^{(n)}(a))^{(m)}(f) - 1^{(n)}(a)$ and $(H(T, f) - 1^{(n)}(b))^{(m)}(f) - 1^{(n)}(b)$ share the same value of $f$, then $H(T, f) - 1^{(n)}(a)$ and $H(T, f) - 1^{(n)}(b)$ share all derivatives, implying

This research presents an updated version of a 1999 algorithm by Cantor and Geisser for solving systems of polynomial equations in two variables, utilizing exponential interpolation, and makes it more efficient when dealing with noisy data. The algorithm is significantly faster in such cases and its correctness under noise is proven, and we offer an alternative approach with comparable results. The presentation of this method is more user-friendly compared to the original algorithm, and we support our ideas with practical examples.

In this research, we present and analyze two types of photon correlations, specifically $g^{(2)}_{\phi}$ and $g^{(2)}_{p}$, in the context of the Jaynes-Cummings model with two photonic channels, one polariton-based and the other phonon-based. By adjusting parameters in this system, the emission of either correlated or anti-correlated photons can be controlled, enabling the creation of various quantum states of light, including non-classical Fock states and squeezed states. Furthermore, the interplay between the coupled cavity and the bus waveguide results in the generation of non-classical correlated photon states, $g^{(2)}_{\phi}$ and $g^{(2)}_{p}$, which can take on positive or negative values, thus exhibiting the characteristic of non-classical light, as opposed to their absolute values which classically can be explained.

By employing ab-initio calculations, we've developed a more accurate equation of
states that better reflects the behavior of matter at extremely high pressures,
particularly at pressures exceeding 100 megapascals, we've discovered that a single
equation can describe various alkali elements, thus validating the concept of
corresponding states. This new equation not only surpasses existing models like the
Bose equation of state, but also aligns with recent high-precision laboratory
measurements, providing a solid theoretical basis for predicting solid behaviors,
including phase transitions, under extremely high-pressure, low-temperature
conditions.

Our calculations of vector meson propagators, specifically for the rho and omega mesons, are conducted within a framework that breaks parity locally, incorporating effects such as the Chern-Simons term and finite baryon density. These calculations are carried out using a variant of the sigma model in the large N_c limit, combined with a self-consistent bridge function method. The interaction between these factors modifies the phase transition involving the rho meson, while also inducing mass shifts in the Chern-Simons mode of both the rho and omega mesons in an environment of finite baryon density.

A network-based problem is addressed with a distributed algorithm that computes the size of an outerplanar network in place and probability, leveraging only local node IDs. By allocating shared counters to each network node, the algorithm allows probabilistic ID sampling and counter adjustment, ultimately determining the network size at a constant factor near optimality.

A novel approach to resolving the Hamiltonian constraint in asymptotically flat spacetimes, particularly those that are conformally flat. Unlike conventional methods that divide the problem into smaller, linked components, this new method directly addresses the constraint without such division. It achieves this by rescaling the conformal factor in a way that transforms the problem into a purely local issue.

The JUNO (Large-scale Liquid Scintillator Detector) experiment, currently under construction at the Yangjiang site in Guangdong, China, is designed to operate with up to 20 kton of liquid scintillator.  Designed to operate as a combined short-baseline neutrino reactor and day/night test, it is intended to utilize 20,000 20-inch PMTs for detecting the 4-m PeV neutrinos that will be used to probe the day/night shift.  This paper will discuss the design of the PLS (Pilot Liquid Detector) that will be used to test the performance of the liquid scintillator and the 20-inch PMTs that will be used in the experiment.  It will also describe the PLS's status as of 2021.

Inference of multidimensional time series future values is crucial across various fields. The challenge lies in capturing complex non-linear patterns across time and space. Existing methods struggle with this, often neglecting important factors. We address this issue by enhancing the Informer model to better handle complex relationships. Our variations, by embedding a multi-head attention mechanism and a residual structure, allow the model to capture hidden patterns more effectively. Through thorough experiments on public and real-world datasets, our model outperformed its competitors and demonstrated better accuracy and efficiency.

Achieving high ADC capabilities requires precise atmospheric models to break down the performance of current systems, but the choice of model can introduce discrepancies of up to 10% in certain wavelength ranges, according to our study. We examined three models, and the one from Dullstein should not be selected as it exhibits the largest errors, particularly outside the visible spectrum. Our research highlights the necessity of incorporating non-water spectra into future models to improve accuracy.

We present Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), a novel training technique that boosts the performance of pre-trained language models by effectively utilizing unused model information and marginal label information. Unlike standard methods, PILE is phase-separated into a one-time model phase and a multi-stage task phase, where it iterates through forward and backward passes to maximize the model's labeled information utilization. Experiments on various NLP tasks reveal that PILE significantly outperforms its competitors by achieving better results with comparable training resources.

We investigate a multi-sensor network's capability to detect ultralight bosonic dark matter-induced stochastic intensity fluctuations. Our research shows that the detection sensitivity of multi-sensor networks can significantly surpass single-sensor performance, and the optimal network configuration can be determined through the maximization of the Fisher information matrix, and subsequently enhanced estimation through joint data analysis of multiple sensors.

The paper investigates the ability of certain nonsymmetric stencils derived from tri-diagonal matrices to facilitate rapid recovery of sparsely Stiffly Stable Oscillatory (SSO) signals, particularly those representing multi-component wave phenomena, through nonlinear sampling methods. It specifically evaluates the efficacy of these stencils in addressing the Basis Pursuit problem, demonstrating that their spectral properties directly impact the accuracy of sparse solution approximation, even in the presence of significant sampling gaps.

The rise of programmable switches has led to a wealth of research in configurable network devices, yet a significant challenge remains: the scarcity of open-source compiler backends hinders further progress. Existing P4 compiler designs face limitations, including incomplete functionality, security vulnerabilities, and hindrance to the development of novel compiler features. To address these issues, we introduce P4Test, a testing framework to enhance the reliability of P4 compiler development. By utilizing formal methods, P4Test verifies the functional correctness of P4 programs by comparing the output of a new compiler with a trusted reference, thereby identifying discrepancies and guiding further improvement. Our approach has been successfully applied to a Metal verifier and PISA compiler, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method in pinpointing issues such as suboptistic pattern matching strategies and compiler crashes.

A new efficient technique for solving the vector Euler equation is developed within the framework of a moving mesh system, leveraging the advantages of a $H(\textrm{div})$-conforming mixed element formulation. By employing the method of characteristics to transform the equation into a pointwise problem and discretizing the resulting linear system on the mesh using a mixed finite element approach, we achieve a more accurate and efficient solution compared to standard methods, particularly in the case of larger time steps. The method's performance is demonstrated through numerical experiments involving flow maps generated by vector fields that change frequently, such as those encountered in electromagnetic simulations.

Machine learning development faces challenges in addressing ethical concerns. 
To address this, we integrate three established methods - performance metrics for 
fairness, federated training and differential privacy for privacy preservation. 
We combine these approaches to create a unified system for privacy-preserving 
machine learning that accounts for fairness and data confidentiality. 
To address the limitations of existing research, we develop a new form of distributed 
privacy measurement. To demonstrate our approach's effectiveness, we test it on 
two standard datasets - German credit and Adult income.

Researchers at the LHCb experiment analyzed combined data, collected in 2011 and 2012, to investigate the $B_c^+$ particle's behavior. The study revealed evidence of two $B_c^+$ excited states, which were identified as having energy levels higher than the ground state by 355 and 415 megaelectronvolts, respectively. The research found that these states match theoretical predictions, with states numbered 1S and either 1P or 2S, and established the confidence in this match to be 99.73 percent in one case and 99.73 percent in the other, based on a chi-squared per degree of freedom comparison.

Researchers have previously adapted single-step Runge-Kutta methods for handling problems with continuous stages, and now this idea has been successfully applied to the Hamiltonian-Verlet-method, a time-discontinuous Runge-Kutta method specifically designed for Hamiltonian problems, as reported in multiple studies including those by Butcher et al., Israr et al., and Lin et al. Building on this connection, new continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods have been developed, specifically for the Hamiltonian problems, and their stage values can be calculated independently, making them suitable for parallel processing, and when applied to isotonic systems, these methods preserve key properties such as symmetry and the area-preserving characteristic, and also extend to non-gradient systems by preserving modified symplectic properties, and an optimal method with two exponential stages has been found, and the method's weights can be determined using quadratic oscillators, and these weights result in high-order accuracy, including results for stages with n=2 to 6, indicating that for any order the accuracy is at least n-2.

Convolutional and recurrent neural networks are typically trained using a stochastic gradient descent algorithm, which utilizes mini-batches of data to minimize prediction errors. Our research introduces batched, local policy optimization for convolutions and recurrences, which leverages the dependency structure within neural network operations to reduce the computation required to update parameter gradients. By applying this method, we demonstrate an $O(\log_2 b)$ speedup in training speed with batch sizes of $b$, yielding acceleration of up to two times with typical image classification and sequence modeling datasets, and even achieve speedups of up to five times with larger dataset sizes.

Chaotic scattering of a particle in a three-dimensional region divided into four interwoven areas leads to basins of final states with complex boundaries that are marginally stable under undamped conditions. Undertaking a numerical investigation, we explore how weak dissipation affects this stability, obtaining the exponent that quantifies this effect. Basins' fringes are also analyzed in relation to the trajectories of an average time until divergence near these fringes. Our study reveals that under weak dissipation, the exponents governing the average time until divergence near these fringes near different fringes are not uniform, exhibiting variations depending on the specific fringes considered.

The muon g-2 anomaly might be explained by a new light particle interacting with the muon, but its production in muon collisions has not been extensively investigated. We propose that the future F2 Muon experiment could effectively explore the parameter space involved in this anomaly through searches for the production of single particles decaying into muon-antimuon pairs or as a resonance in the muon-antimuon invariant mass spectrum. Both options offer the advantage of being experimentally feasible and distinguishable from the background noise, ultimately contributing to clarifying the nature of the anomaly.

Human Activity Net, a two-step activity recognition model, synergizes hand-crafted and learned features to outperform current state-of-the-art in related tasks. Its architecture is built on a spatial-temporal attention mechanism that pinpoints key spatial regions and weight their importance across videos. Additionally, this mechanism adjusts its weights dynamically during time, accumulating them to emphasize dominant patterns. Research shows HAN effectively identifies inter-frame variations and enhanced activity visibility. Further analysis validates HAN's capacity to integrate the strengths of both feature types, and our experiments demonstrate its compatibility with various backbone networks.

We've investigated the outcome of scattering an electromagnetic wave off both near-extremal and extremal black holes. Our findings show that for near-extremal black holes, the incident pulse is fully absorbed as the hole's horizon shrinks to zero, whereas for extremal black holes, the horizon does not contract, resulting in the creation of an infinite number of increasingly thin pulses that persist forever. These new pulses are exponentially weaker than the original, specifically $e^{-\kappa_v l/(v-1)}$ times as intense, where $v$ represents the time elapsed after the initial interaction, $\kappa_v$ is the pulsation of the pulse, and $l$ denotes the angular momentum quantum number. Our analysis also reveals that these secondary pulses are directed towards the south pole of the horizon's angular coordinates, whereas the initial pulse was centered at the equator. Our research further indicates that the time-dependent backreaction of the pulse on the metric is analogous to the perturbation of a scalar field, provided that the pulse's frequency $\kappa_v$ is greater than zero. Our findings are consistent with the hypothesis proposed in the arXiv:1902.09479 paper.

Star formation research is crucial to understanding our origins in the cosmos, and as astronomers, we strive to uncover how the stars we observe today relate to the processes occurring out of sight, both now and in the past. The regions where stars are born shroud critical events within them, and this also applies to the cosmos' darkest areas, where supernovae occur, obscuring their underlying dynamics. The same principle applies to the cosmos, and this also applies to the cosmos, and this also applies to the cosmos.

When calculating entropy for a probability distribution, a problem arises if there is no direct way to calculate the probability values. To overcome this limitation, the differential intersection method was developed to calculate entropy from samples, provided the joint distribution of any two variables can be calculated. However, this method is sample-biased and biased even when the variables' relationship is known, which is the case for many common probability distributions. A new bias-correcting approach based on the k-nearest neighbor method was proposed and demonstrated to effectively correct the bias in scenarios involving joint and marginal entropies, as well as mutual information. This approach shows particular promise in the analysis of neuroimaging data, particularly fMRI, where estimating the entropy from simulated and real datasets has been achieved and compared to existing methods.
