We have demonstrated the converse of Dehner's finding by showing that every $t$-chromatic graph containing a $K_t$-minor with one of its parts attached to a vertex whose neighborhood within that part is fully connected actually has a $K_{t-1}$-minor with two parts, with one of its parts attached to a vertex whose neighborhood within that part is fully connected.

Similarly, it was found that every such $t$-chromatic graph with one-part eliminable $K_t$-minors actually has a $K_{t-1}$-minor with one additional part, with one of its parts attached to a vertex whose neighborhood within that part is fully connected, and one-part eliminable.

This research investigates an adaptive cost-reducing algorithm, defining its efficiency based on how quickly it approaches optimality as it evolves. Surprisingly, the type of bound used to measure convergence—whether it's for all possible inputs or just under certain conditions—can be directly influenced by the algorithm's own adjustments, even if the given descent bound doesn't. Furthermore, we find that using an algorithm, even one designed for a different purpose, can improve the rate of convergence, as long as the rate is defined as the best possible outcome, also known as the optimality gap.

The process of single-photon generation through atomic interactions is typically randomized, limiting its applications in precision measurement. However, if the collisions are initiated in a controlled manner, as suggested by experiments using controlled release mechanisms, it is possible to significantly enhance this limitation. Our research focuses on entangling two atoms through controlled, controlled, and random triggering of entangling collisions, comparing the states produced and their associated quantum metrological sensitivity. We found that triggering the collisions in a controlled manner yields a superior sensitivity relative to random triggering, while also producing distinct states from a combination of controlled and random triggering. Furthermore, by strategically controlling the collisions, it is possible to obtain any desired superposition of entangled and anti-entangled states, which can be utilized in various quantum information processing tasks.

This research investigates the behavior of the lowest energy state of a nonlinear differential equation known as the anisotropic $p$-Laplace eigenvalue problem under specific boundary conditions influenced by a parameter $\beta$. By drawing on the principles of the isoperimetric inequality and a specialized inequality by Hardy, we establish precise limits on this eigenvalue, particularly how it changes with variations in the parameter $\beta$ and another dimension-related parameter $N$. We also examine its implications in a scenario of increasingly restrictive boundary conditions, illustrating the problem's adaptability to different situations.

Recent research has introduced Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) as a flexible framework, unifying traditional CNNs and fully connected neural networks. However, applying GCNs to real-world problems often involves creating arbitrary graph representations, which can be cumbersome and problem-specific. To address this limitation, we present a new approach that automatically generates problem-independent graph representations by leveraging the proximity of unsupervised pretraining. The method uses proximity, derived from contrastive learning, to define node connections and guides GCN pretraining through contrastive objectives that minimize representation distortion during network transformations. Results demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the efficacy of GCNs on various datasets, including Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed, MNIST, and CelebA, yielding improvements in AUC scores and other performance metrics.

This work presents an enhanced contextualized self-training algorithm, Deep Contextualized Self-training (DCST), for tackling parsing issues. Unlike conventional self-training, which relies on local information, DCST leverages model-based predictions and contextual cues to refine existing models more effectively. Furthermore, building on recent work that utilizes graph-based dependency parses to optimize model parameters, we have developed a similar evaluation metric that incorporates predicted distributional information, thereby enabling deeper evaluation and training of models. Experimental results for several English parsing datasets have demonstrated that DCST consistently surpasses the best existing self-training techniques and significantly improves the baseline performance.

Using 36.1 fb^-1 of proton-proton collision data, collected at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV with the CMS experiment, we investigate the rare charmless three-body decays of the B meson, specifically focusing on B to D(l+ nu_l) where l can be a electron, muon, or a tau, and a D consists of either two pions, a pion and a kaon, or two kaons. Our analysis is based on a large sample of events and we find that the expected accuracy for measuring these rare decays is around 1% for electron and muon modes, and approximately 20% for the tau mode due to the significantly higher production rate in the tau modes. Our results show that the expected precision for these measurements exceeds existing world records by a large margin, with the exception of two previously measured B to K and D*+ (l+ nu_l) where we find that the measured frequencies align with the predictions made by the Standard Model, exhibiting only a minor discrepancy in the case of a muon, which is well within the calculated uncertainty margins.

A general, broad approach has been developed to define and calculate the properties of field theory symmetries that are not necessarily reversible, using an adaptation of topological techniques to accommodate higher-dimensional contexts. This approach can be applied to a wide range of theories, including those featuring electric-magnetic duality, gamma symmetry, and various other phenomena, often requiring the consideration of infinite sequences of related concepts. To manage this complexity, a new, streamlined method has been introduced to derive the necessary fusion rules. Furthermore, a way to determine the associated anyon content has also been introduced. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through detailed applications to specific theories, including two- and four-dimensional examples, with some predictions confirmed by existing research. Additionally, the method provides new insights into the underlying mechanisms of these theories, as seen in the analysis of four-dimensional $U(1)$ gauge theory with a discrete theta term and 2d theories derived from free level-$k$ bosons under modular $T$ and $S$ transformations.

We are investigating whether a solution exists for systems of linear equations, where both coefficients and solutions can take part in Unordered Linear Logic. This is defined over an abelian group that satisfies the discrete dyadic halving property, using a finite field with a prime number of elements $p$, where $p$ is either very small or very large. The complexity of $p$ significantly influences the capabilities of the logic. If $p$ is a relatively small number, a polynomial-time algorithm can decide the satisfiability of such logic formulas, whereas, if $p$ is a very large number, the problem becomes extremely difficult to solve, with polynomial-time Turing machines only able to solve it in an extremely high polynomial time, under a polynomial-time Turing access to the $p$-th root finding problem in $\mathbb{F}_p$. This indicates that the satisfiability problem for these unordered linear equations is in a relatively low complexity class when $p$ is a very large number, assuming the $p$-th root finding problem in $\mathbb{F}_p$ is in a relatively low complexity class. This result is surprising, as it shows that eliminating order relations from decision problems can sometimes make them easier to solve, even if it significantly increases the time required to find a solution.

The valence and optical spectra of (Eu_1-xBi_x)2Ir_2O_7 single crystals were experimentally studied through photoemission spectroscopy for various compositions where the bismuth level ranges from x = 0.05 to x = 0.20. As Bismuth is substituted, the valence band, primarily composed of 6d states, shifts towards lower binding energies, whereas changes in the conduction band states were not observed. As Bismuth is substituted, the material transitions from exhibiting insulating behavior to exhibiting a series of quantum phase transitions, ultimately becoming a superconductor at x = 0.15. Notably, the conduction band remains unaffected by these transitions, suggesting that the emergence of superconductivity is linked to alterations in the 6s states.

Given positive integers $a_1, \dots, a_n$, the tuple is termed nontransitive if the strictly inequivalent cyclic permutations occur less frequently than the original tuple when randomly arranged side by side with other random arrangements. Specifically, a nontransitive $k$-tuple exists for sufficiently large integers as long as each element in the tuple is relatively prime to $k$. Additionally, nontransitive $(k_1, k_2, k_3)$-tuples exist for an infinite number of prime values $k$ where the modulo conditions for $k_1, k_2, k_3$ alternate in a specific cyclic pattern. The existence of nontransitive tuples with the largest element two units larger than the smallest was previously established in the case of three-tuples. However, the question of their existence when the largest is one unit larger than the smallest remained unresolved. The present study confirms their existence when the largest is one unit larger than the smallest in the case of five-tuples with specific modulo residues. The study also demonstrates an algorithmic method to generate nontransitive tuples under specific, relatively prime modulo conditions.

A run-time option enables users to adjust system behavior at run-time by modifying configuration. Linux kernel options are run-time settings that can be changed without re-compiling the OS. Although flexible, these options can introduce unneeded complexity, security vulnerabilities, and performance issues when activated. It's possible, but difficult, to disable unused run-time options, which often remain enabled by default. This report introduces RTOMiner, a static analysis tool that identifies and removes unused run-time options in C systems like the Linux kernel. RTOMiner is evaluated on multiple versions of the Linux kernel, which are then compared to manual analysis results to demonstrate its reliability. By collaborating with Linux kernel developers, RTOMiner is used to automatically disable a set of options prior to each release, which may enhance security and efficiency.

A comprehensive ionisation detector is ideal for detecting nuclear recoils resulting from dark matter interactions, leveraging the distinct ionisation signatures of such events. Researchers have previously established the theoretical framework and simulation tools for recoil-induced ionisation, but a crucial aspect - the calculation of energy loss in semi-relativistic regimes - was missing. This work presents a new ionisation loss formula suitable for such speeds, which is then incorporated into the existing simulation code, now known as GEANT4-GDML. GDML is an extended version of the standard GEANT4, incorporating an updated ionisation model and tailored for gravitational-wave observatories, particularly the Einstein Telescope.

In this research, we present an innovative quantum teleportation protocol that utilizes ultra-high-rate, room-temperature entangled anti-polariton qubit states as a shared resource between the sender and the receiver. The proposed protocol's fidelity can surpass that of traditional methods employing faithful measurements and classical communication, even when the high-rate entangled qubit state's fidelity is less than perfect. The enhanced fidelity of the teleported quantum state allows us to successfully execute bell-state analysis, a critical component in generating large-scale, room-temperature entangled photon states via spontaneous parametric down-conversion, thereby bypassing the need for complex refrigeration systems and expensive equipment, and potentially allowing for the development of scalable quantum technologies.

A key aspect of cardiac health assessment is analyzing inter-beat intervals (IBIs) derived from electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. Despite advancements in signal processing, extracting reliable IBI from noisier versions of ECG signals recorded on consumer-grade devices remains challenging. This research addresses this gap by developing a novel deep-learning approach that utilizes dilated convolutional neural networks to accurately detect R-peaks in ECG signals, even when they contain significant noise levels. By combining this with a simple yet effective pre-processing step, our method achieves robust performance across ECG signals recorded on various devices, at multiple noise levels, and across a diverse range of individuals. Our results show that our approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving a 99.4% average accuracy for IBI estimation, even when estimating cardiac parameters such as heart rate variability.

We investigated the active system governed by Maritan et al.'s model, characterized by active forces generated from random on/off point sources tied to the system's deviation from equilibrium position. The effective temperature was determined by applying the fluctuation-dissipation theorem to compare system responses with fluctuations. In harmonic potentials, we found that only equal-amplitude activation breaks thermal equilibrium, resulting in temperature variations depending on the activation ratio and relaxation time specific to each observable. However, in anharmonic potentials, temperature variations depend also on the system's potential curvature. Additionally, in such anharmonic scenarios, the fluctuation-dissipation theorem is inadequate for defining effective temperature, as different fluctuations exhibit distinct non-equilibrium temperature values.

HUMBI is a novel approach to building realistic 3D models of human expressions using a large dataset called the Human-OBS dataset, which captures subtle facial expressions in a controlled environment. This dataset consists of real-time 4K facial videos captured using a special camera system, along with real-time expression feedback, to capture a wide range of expressions from real people. HUMBL utilizes a specialized approach called real-time expression transfer to transfer expressions from a source person to a target person, allowing for the creation of a diverse range of expressions from just a few examples. This allows for the creation of a realistic 3D representation of human expressions, which can be used for a variety of applications, including special effects, therapy, and more.

Developing a unified language understanding model across multiple languages is a difficult task, particularly when dealing with languages that have limited resources. Resources like data and computational capabilities are to blame. To overcome these limitations, we've developed a new, data-efficient, and economically friendly approach to training multi-language models. We leverage pre-trained monolingual models, then combine their inputs in a shared space, allowing us to train one model for many languages using just a little labeled data. We've tested this approach on 12 languages and seen a significant improvement in performance when compared to other similar methods.

BasicVSR++ is an enhanced version of BasicVSR that we developed. By integrating BasicVSR's core idea, BasicVSR++ achieves significant improvements over its predecessor. We achieved a 0.65% increase in PSNR and 1.2 times better computational efficiency compared to BasicVSR. Furthermore, BasicVSR++ outperforms other state-of-the-art methods while maintaining better efficiency.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, objects often appear in various forms across different tasks, which can be seen as different instances of the same dynamic object, yet existing methods struggle to distinguish between different objects' dynamics. Current models adopt a single learned dynamics for all objects, which hinders generalization to novel objects' dynamics. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that utilizes visual cues to identify specific objects and their respective dynamics, which are then integrated into an attention-based Q-function to facilitate multi-object interaction. Through a multi-head attention mechanism, our method enables the model to selectively focus on multiple objects, which in turn aids in multi-task reinforcement learning. Experimental results demonstrate the improved performance of our approach in multi-task settings, as well as its efficient few-shot learning capabilities.

We've investigated a range of scenarios, both in alignment with and diverging from the standard conditions of detailed balance, in order to optimize the performance of heat engines and thermal batteries when coupled with small-scale heat-conducting systems. Our models incorporate various interactions between these devices and stochastic fluctuations in the applied forces, all of which adhere to the fluctuation theorem. We've found that, in scenarios where the protocol follows detailed balance, increasing the scaling parameter λ will consistently improve performance up to a certain point, at which the maximum achievable limit can be described using traditional thermodynamic relations. We've also demonstrated that, even when the protocol deviates from the rules of detailed balance, the dependency of performance on λ still exhibits a similar peak, although the asymptotic behavior may be influenced by specific characteristics of the protocol. We've identified the conditions under which the performance, both as heat engine and thermal battery, will respond in a unimodal manner to changes in λ, effectively creating a simplified framework in non-equilibrium thermodynamics.

This research proposes a new approach to simulate the impact of historical hurricanes on power grids by combining three data sources: hurricane tracks, generator historical outage records, and SCADA data for real-time grid monitoring. These simulations are carried out using a random walk method to model historical hurricane tracks, a binary classification algorithm to predict generator outages, and an optimization technique to recover the grid. The results demonstrate the potential of this method to improve resilience planning and provide a data-driven reference for the future.
We derive a version of Hadamard's three circles theorem for monogenic functions across $R^{n+1}$, as well as an equivalent logarithmic convexity result.

A generalization of the dyck languages, initially defined by McNaughton and Sasaki in 1965, has been applied to the theory of dynamical systems since the 1990s. This concept initially emerged from the study of homeomorphisms on surfaces with specific patterns. However, recent developments have shown that it can now be applied to more complex scenarios, such as the study of codings associated with special invariant sets of the unit interval under various piecewise affine maps. We will explore these recent outcomes, which demonstrate that the natural coding systems for two types of newly introduced piecewise affine maps - the generalized sawtooth map and the inverse generalized sawtooth map - are directly related to the dyck systems. Additionally, we will discuss how these findings have led to the resolution of specific mathematical problems concerning the Hausdorff dimensions of certain attractors associated with these maps.

High-energy colliders of the near future, including abeV colliders, will provide a highly sensitive test for particle physics models featuring complex new phenomena. Even heavier particles can be detected even if the high-energy collider can't directly produce them in a collision, as they can manifest in decays of produced particles. Even if the collider's energy is lower than the mass of the new particles, they can still be detected through subtle distortions in the decay products' momentum distribution. We examine the ability of an advanced Higgs collider to detect models of new particles over a vast range of masses, considering various scenarios. Our research focuses on the simplified model of a Higgs portal to dark matter and compares it to other models in terms of the most restrictive test that can be done at different types of colliders.

A hierarchical model was developed to enhance the representation of complex periodic signals, such as human speech, by leveraging its inherent nested structure, where individual signal components exhibit their own distinct frequency patterns. Increasing the network's depth allows it to capture a broader range of these inherent hierarchies. This study investigates the utility of hierarchical models in capturing speech characteristics, utilizing a specific aspect of human voice - the voice onset time (VOT) as a starting point, and then expanding to a more comprehensive analysis of the speech signal's mel-spectrogram. Our findings indicate that a hierarchical model can efficiently capture speech signal characteristics with minimal units, and that a deeper network can result in enhanced outcomes.

This paper introduces a USB-Coded Factorization Biclustering approach to Collaborative Filtering, which overcomes the limitations of biclustering-based CF methods that struggle with sparsity and lack of a clear model for user/item preferences. Our method enhances existing UBFC algorithms, such as ABCF, through three main advancements: employing Biclustering Factorization to model user/item embeddings, using USB-coding for accurate and diverse bicommatrices, and applying Bayesian optimization for optimal results. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which outperforms comparable biclustering-based CF methods in addressing sparsity issues.

The objective of this study is to enhance our understanding of the star AD Leo's magnetic activity and its effects on its surface and atmosphere. Utilizing data from high-resolution spectra captured with the VLT/UVES spectrograph, our research focuses on high-activity periods experienced by AD Leo between 2012 and 2014. By analyzing line profiles of specific iron and chromium lines, we have identified features that could serve as more accurate indicators of magnetic activity compared to the conventional H-alpha index. Additionally, we have used synthetic spectra to determine optimal wavelengths where variability is most influenced by activity-induced changes, discovering new star-specific indices centered around these wavelengths that exhibit superior sensitivity and signal-to-noise ratio compared to the traditional photometric indices.

Advanced quantum sensors are essential for resolving the ongoing controversy surrounding topological superconductivity, particularly in distinguishing between true Non-Abelian Majorana modes and non-topological counterparts. To address this limitation, we propose the utilization of a hybrid quantum sensor, combining a double quantum dot system and an ancillary microwave cavity, to detect and measure finite temperature distributions in d-wave superconductor/ferromagnet/superconductor junctions. The proposed setup enables the implementation of thermo-cycling protocols, facilitating the characterization of finite temperature spectra and increasing signal strength by reducing thermal noise through conditional measurement and cavity damping.

Building on the work of Arone, Blumberg, and Mandel, this article establishes a framework linking topological Hochschild homology to the concept of shadows within bicategorical structures. It-braids together techniques from condensed homological algebra and stable homotopy theory, resulting in a flexible tool for adapting THH to various contexts. The research also explores applications of this framework to iterated topological Hochschild homology and a categorical version of topological K-theory, with implications for the spectrum of letters, letters with coefficients, and bicategorical $K$-theory.

This research introduces a novel encoding technique that captures an image's artistic style using an arrow-like structure, which is more effective than other methods like PCA or VAE. By leveraging Strehblow's analysis of style transfer, the encoding technique takes advantage of the separation of style and content in four-dimensional space, resulting in a compact and informative style representation. The technique's performance is evaluated using clustering, content preservation, and artistic evaluation metrics, which demonstrate its superiority over other encoding methods.

The traditional approach to mapping videos to semantic maps is hindered by its inability to handle temporal data and its reliance on manually annotated semantic maps. In response, we propose an unsupervised cross-modal attentional alignment of videos and semantic maps, which enables the creation of meaningful semantic maps from raw data. Our method involves two key innovations: Firstly, we incorporate a context-ground module within the attentional mapping process to incorporate neighbor information from the semantic maps into each individual annotation. Secondly, we incorporate an attentional auto-encoder that learns to compress spatial patterns while retaining modality-specific details. Our extensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our method in producing high-quality semantic maps and its outperformance over existing unsupervised and semi-supervised approaches.

This research explores how the settling velocity of snow particles, within a specified range of 0.01 to 0.1 Stokes numbers, is influenced by varying turbulent intensity levels, measured by Inflection-Richness factors of 0.5, 0.75, and 0.95. To achieve this, a series of direct numerical simulations were conducted, involving four distinct combinations of these variables. These simulations were performed using two different aspect ratios, 4 and 6, in 256^3 numerical grids. The obtained settling velocities, when normalized, demonstrate minimal fluctuation with fluctuations around 20% and an average standard deviation of 6.4%. This indicates that snow particle clustering is largely unaffected by turbulence or grid resolutions, within the tested Stokes numbers.

Significant progress in deep learning has significantly enhanced the ability of generative models to capture the intricacies of real-world data. This progress has been further accelerated by advances in high-performance computing. Our project leverages the latest advancements in generative models, including variational autoencoders, normalizing flows, and auto-regressive models, to restore, transform, and synthesize images of exoplanets and small molecules. To evaluate our model's performance, we employ a combination of quantitative and qualitative metrics, analyzing both restored and synthesized data. Notably, the synthesized images of small molecules exhibit remarkable detail, rivaling existing high-resolution databases.

This research introduces a data compression method rooted in deep learning, specifically a convolutional autoencoder (CAE) approach, to compress and restore image data. The objective is to develop an efficient method for simultaneously compressing data and ensuring its quality post-decompression. Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE), a novel autoencoder variant, surpasses existing CAE-based compression methods. The BCAE model features a pioneering autoencoder structure, enabling superior compression quality and faster processing speeds. Furthermore, BCAE exhibits enhanced robustness against noise, leading to the recovery of high-quality images. The BCAE model also boasts a reduced parameter count, thereby improving its computational efficiency.

This research paper presents the results of a thermodynamic analysis conducted on Coma galaxy cluster data obtained from ROSAT All-Sky Survey measurements of temperature and Einstein's radius. Prior to the study, a beta model was applied to deconvolute the data, and notable temperature variations were identified in distinct regions. Gyroscopic phase transitions were discovered at specific thresholds of cluster radius, which were then examined in the context of thermodynamic consequences. These consequences include emergent critical properties, continuous phase transitions, and varying thermodynamic behaviors in different system regions. The study further highlights potential applications of its findings, which could offer a more in-depth understanding of the CMB primary anisotropy and provide valuable insights for the Coma cluster's study.

To contextually understand this problem, we should first comprehend the concept of geometric hypergraphs, particularly convex geometric hypergraphs, and the challenges associated with them, including saturation problems and the calculation of saturation numbers. In the realm of convex geometric hypergraphs, a new saturation issue and its corresponding numerical value are introduced and analyzed. Specific examples and exact calculations of saturation numbers are provided for distinct geometric hypergraph structures, including those influenced by set patterns, circle configurations, and point arrangements in the plane.

This research explores direct particle-to-alpha cluster reactions with intermediate energies, focusing on the (p, p') and (d, 3He') processes off the isotopes $^{12}$C and $^{14}$N. Cross-section measurements were conducted at 209 MeV using the TACITE spectrometer at AN2M. Detected signals from the excited states of $^{12}$C and $^{14}$N revealed notable direct reaction cross-sections. Notably, the reaction cross-sections for deuterons were significantly higher than those for alpha particles, with a ratio of approximately 10. Detailed analysis of the angular energy distributions of the excited states was performed, with configurations derived from wave functions based on the composition of the components, with the Deformed Shell Model (Deformed Shell Model) being the primary constituent. Calculated cluster form factors were in good agreement with the experimental data. Calculated B(E2) values were compared with existing literature and demonstrated a significant discrepancy.

The Trident system, comprising three rotating discs in a fluid environment, mimics the movement of certain aquatic animals by generating a steady stream of vortices in its wake. By fine-tuning the spinning speed relative to the forward movement, specific types of vortex ring structures can be produced, and this is known as the Stewartesson number. At a particular range of this number, both the forward movement and spinning cannot be separately controlled, but instead, changing the spinning speed directly impacts the vortex ring structure in its wake, and this, in turn, determines the speed of forward movement. Our study investigates the mechanics of load-driven movement in the Stewartesson number range, and how the vortex ring structure in its wake can be utilized to optimize its propulsion under various loading conditions. Through simulations, we discovered that the disc system, under light loading, produces efficient vortex rings that provide strong thrust, but as the loading increases, the system's interaction yields suboptimal vortex rings, resulting in reduced thrust and increased drag, ultimately leading to decreased forward progress.

This study investigates the combined effects of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy on colon cancer and the associated immune response through mathematical modeling. Doxorubicin reduces tumor cells, but also harms immune cells, whereas IL-2 boosts the tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. The models' predictions were validated against in vivo data from a mouse model, specifically assessing the impact on tumor cells, blood T-cells, and plasma Doxorubicin levels. Optimal control models of the therapy were developed to minimize the tumor cell population while limiting the exposure of healthy cells to Doxorubicin. The results indicate that the combination of Doxorubicin and IL-2 can enhance the anti-tumor response and the efficacy of the treatment, particularly the recruitment of CD8+ T-cells, which are vital for combating the tumor.

This study investigates the relationship between the freshness of information and system capacity in wireless communications. We demonstrate that improving system capacity does not necessarily lead to lower information delay. We examine a scenario where a single-source, single-destination communication system uses either direct transmission or a decode-and-forward relay method with opportunistic scheduling to maximize throughput while minimizing delay. Direct transmission results in minimal age at the destination when the source schedules based on the oldest information packet. In the relay scenario, if the source and relay schedules independently, the same outcome occurs; however, if the relay schedules after the source, optimal performance requires coordinated scheduling. Coordinated scheduling yields lower average information delay compared to independent scheduling.

This research paper investigates whether helicity is conserved for a specific set of weak solutions to the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, defined in a certain function space. We establish the conservation of helicity for these solutions, provided the initial condition meets specific requirements. Our approach involves approximating the given weak solution using a sequence of smooth, divergence-free vector fields that are also smooth and bounded. These vector fields serve as building blocks for the given weak solution, and we show that they also satisfy the conservation of helicity for their respective initial conditions. By leveraging this property, we establish the conservation of helicity for the given weak solution, defined in a certain function space. Our results expand the class of weak solutions for which helicity is consided in a significant way.

Assessments related to the asymptotic behavior of Scudlo's functional are made, 
in connection with compactly supported Hamiltonians typically employed in 
geometrical optics, leading to enhanced mathematical aptitudes.
This results in the formulation of more precise analytical expressions, 
specifically in terms of the L^2-norm.

We've investigated how the orbital eccentricities of compact binary systems evolve over time, taking into account that their eccentricities can't be ignored, unlike previously assumed. This was done within the framework of second-generation eccentric-orbital gravitational waves. Our work involved developing an efficient and accurate method to simulate these systems using specially designed software, which we've integrated into existing simulation packages. These simulations have been carried out for various mass combinations of binary systems, across a range of initial orbits and eccentricities, to determine the resulting eccentricities at the point of detection by gravitational-wave interferometers. Our findings indicate that final eccentricities are highly dependent on those at the start of the system's life, with an increased eccentricity leading to higher eccentricity at the point of detection. Our work also highlights that there's a range of initial eccentricities where the system evolves more slowly, allowing for a more gradual increase in eccentricity.

A new type of high-energy X-ray source, the extended free-electron laser oscillator (XFELO), promises to provide ultra-short, high-intensity X-ray pulses. To achieve the necessary conditions for generating these pulses, we've developed a seeding method combined with an electron multiplier, which boosts the current and enables higher output intensities. In addition, we've optimized the device's interaction with a magnetic field to maximize its performance. Our research shows that the XFELO can generate an X-ray pulse with a duration of 50 femtoseconds, an energy of 3 millijoules, and a peak intensity of around 10^18 W/cm^2, all of which can be consistently produced at a high rate of 10 Hz.

Predicting node events in dynamic graphs is a critical challenge. Existing methods utilize historical node interactions to anticipate future occurrences, yet they often neglect the underlying connections within the graph, hindering their effectiveness. To address this limitation, we propose a dual-path model, named DyGED, that simultaneously considers node sequences and graph structures for event prediction. First, we develop an event prediction module that uses historical node interactions to predict upcoming events. Next, we propose a feedback mechanism that creates and predicts event sequences, after which our model learns the underlying graph structures through an attention-based process. Finally, we design a model optimization strategy that leverages predicted events to guide the model in capturing graph patterns. Experimental results demonstrate that DyGED outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches, especially in scenarios involving sparse or evolving graphs.

A new approach is developed for validating hydrodynamic models using the self-similar Guderley problem. This involves adapting the classic solution to hydrodynamic explosions with solid boundaries to a scenario where the boundary infalls freely. As a result, the material properties and state at any point in time can be accurately determined without numerical computations. By comparing these analytical values to those obtained through numerical simulations, key aspects such as mass flux and entropy production can be effectively quantify their generation. Additionally, various aspects of the Guderley solution can be utilized as input for other hydrodynamic scenarios, such as driving inflows for stellar evolution simulations or artificial mixtures for supernova simulations.

In the past few years, the concept of explainable AI has gained significant attention due to its importance in addressing the lack of transparency in AI systems. Although various RL methods have been proposed, there is a scarcity of research focusing on the role of requirements engineering in enhancing explainable AI from a system designer's perspective. This study seeks to fill this knowledge gap by incorporating natural language processing and text mining techniques in the process of requirement creation, aiming to automatically detect and include relevant explanations in the overall XR process.

Recent advancements in deep neural networks have significantly enhanced the field of computer-aided diagnosis, particularly in endoscopic imaging. A recent study employed these advancements to evaluate and predict specific characteristics of colorectal polyps using a dataset from the Kaggle Challenge. The researchers developed a framework that utilized transfer learning-based deep neural networks to analyze endoscopic images, and through experimentation, identified the characteristics that could be accurately predicted. The results demonstrated high levels of accuracy, with the classification of colorectal adenomas achieving an Area Under the Curve score of 0.89, the grading of pit pattern pit formation reaching an Area Under the Curve score of 0.81, and the detection of deep invagination scoring an accuracy of 73%. The findings also highlighted the importance of selecting appropriate image preprocessing methods and fine-tuning pre-trained networks to optimize network performance.

A specific type of source code, known as fixed-length source code, was initially analyzed by C. Fong and R. G. Gallager in 1974. They focused on minimizing a specific metric, the average leakage of information about a source message in the codebook to a potential adversary. More recently, the concept of optimal leakage in relation to optimal compression rates for specific types of source codes was revisited and generalized in a 2018 study by T. Taninaka and co-authors. In this paper, the researchers extend their previous findings to analysis of variable-length source codes while also considering how code design can be optimized in light of potential data breaches.

We introduce MrSARP, a novel Markovian synthetic image prior at multi-resolution level, which enables us to generate high-quality images at different resolutions by exploiting the relationship between them. Our proposed hierarchical deep-Gaussian model comprises multiple layers of conditional Gaussian processes, with each level conditioned by the representation at the level below, thus allowing us to leverage the structure at lower resolutions to synthesize images at higher resolutions. We evaluated MrSARP through image restoration experiments and compared it to other image priors in terms of its ability to synthesize clean images from noisy inputs. Our results demonstrate that MrSARP excels at generating high-fidelity images at various resolutions, surpassing other hierarchical image priors in noisy image restoration tasks.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a prominent method for tackling combinatorial optimization problems, yet it introduces complex variational optimization tasks after generating an initial solution. Since the QAOA circuit's complexity grows with the number of variables, its optimization becomes extremely difficult, often exceeding current capabilities. Drawing inspiration from successful applications of Bayesian optimization in quantum systems, we develop a novel approach that integrates Bayesian optimization with the QAOA for more efficient solving of these problems. Our method demonstrates that Bayesian optimization can efficiently navigate the high-dimensional QAOA landscape, and we show that it can also quickly converge to robust performance levels by optimizing a reduced QAOA circuit before transferring the settings to the full QAOA circuit.

We have developed an algorithm to identify all points where two ellipses intersect by decomposing the problem into simpler subtasks. To achieve this, we utilize two established methods: one for solving a four-point equation representing two overlapping spheres, and another for factorizing quadratic equations. Our analysis demonstrates that the new algorithm outperforms the existing geometric approach in terms of both computational speed and numerical stability.

Actor-critic algorithms, a class of reinforcement learning methods, simplify the calculation of the density function for the Gibbs measure produced by the policy's $q$-function. This paper compares three actor-critic algorithms - natural gradient policy update, score function estimate, and GPEU - and examines their behavior during recurrent neural network reinforcement learning updates. Our research reveals that the actor-critic algorithms map the Gibbs measure update in distinct ways: CGP updates the mean directly, SFE leaves the covariance unchanged, and GPBU updates both the mean and covariance independently, causing discrepancies in their behaviors, particularly for SFE and GPBU which can result in convergence to suboptimal stationary points. To address these issues, the author proposes an approach for estimating the Gibbs measure update, which is shown to coincide with the GPEU method under specific conditions.

This study investigates stripe order in the half-filled Hubbard model, specifically focusing on conditions near the boundary where it coexists with antiferromagnetic order. Our analysis demonstrates that stripe order is not merely an effect of reduced quantum fluctuations due to weak hopping amplitudes, but rather that quantum fluctuations play a pivotal role in stabilizing it. By employing a mean-field approach that incorporates corrections up to fourth order quantum fluctuations via a diagrammatic method, we found that such corrections positively influence the stripe order's stability. Conversely, quantum fluctuations negatively impact the antiferromagnetic order, thereby providing an explanation for why the stripe order's critical temperature is typically lower than that of the antiferromagnetic order.

A novel deep learning approach for automatically locating and counting vertebrae in sagittal spinal MRI scans has been developed. This method utilizes a hybrid model combining a 2D U-Net and an attention-based mechanism to accurately identify vertebrae at various levels. By attaching an attention module after convolutional layers, the model can filter out irrelevant information and reduce noise. Experimental results on the publicly available MedSegMN Challenge dataset demonstrate the efficacy of this method, with a 15% improvement in mean absolute error compared to the second-best performing solution, and comparable results to state-of-the-art vertebra identification techniques.

This study utilizes the algebraic and topological framework of Markovian models to analyze complex systems with numerous degrees of freedom, leveraging this framework to simplify and streamline the computation of asymptotic averages and correlation integrals.

We have computed the Hodge-Deligne numbers, or relative $I$-functions, for toric complete intersections with smooth divisors. It is shown that the divisors' relative $I$-functions, when scaled by a specific factor, form a functional equation, with the exception of a single point, which we interpret using Grothendieck's trace formula, given that the divisor is defined by a polynomial of a specific form. Furthermore, for such divisors defined by a polynomial of a specific form, the relative $I$-functions, when divided by their respective series, are equal, and this extends to divisors defined by the same form of expression in the ring.

This paper explores how composites of piezoelectric and resistive materials can be designed to be scale-invariant, allowing for the transmission of mechanical vibrations and electric currents to be fully transmitted across different scales. A piezoelectric-fiber-in-polymer-matrix system is analyzed in detail, where the interaction between the fiber and the surrounding material is examined. A set of conditions is derived that ensures full vibration and electrical conduction transmission between the components, which leads to the development of a reduced-order model for the system's dynamic behavior. Furthermore, it is shown that the optimal polymer resistivity needed to achieve this conduction condition decreases exponentially as the fiber radius gets smaller, and that the dynamic model can be expanded to include higher-order effects to better match the system's actual response.

The interaction between excitons and photons in a microcavity creates a unique optical system that can be finely manipulated. By combining this with SLM technology, complex excitation patterns can be projected onto the microcavity, allowing for precise control over the outcome. This capability enables the exploration of novel phenomena such as multi-point polariton condensation, coherent laser scattering, and the generation of coherent pixel arrays.

The planet K2-22 b, which may be similar to Earth in size, orbits very closely to its host star, resulting in it potentially being exposed to intense XUV radiation. To assess whether this planet can sustain its atmosphere over time, the research team examined the possibility of the planet's XUV exposure. By analyzing the planet's orbit and the likelihood of its host star's XUV radiation, the scientists discovered that this planet likely receives a significant amount of XUV radiation. Utilizing the observed properties of the planet and applying mass loss calculations, the researchers estimated the loss of the planet's mass to be around 0.35 to 0.65 Earth masses per billion years, which could potentially lead to the complete stripping of the planet's atmosphere within its lifetime.

Consider a non-constant polynomial, F, in the variable vector a from the n-dimensional space, with coefficients drawn from the ring of multivariate polynomials b_1 to b_n within the n-dimensional space. These coefficients define a map from n+1 dimensional space to (n+1) dimensional space. Excluding a few points in n+1 dimensional space, each value v in 1-dimensional space results in a singularity for the equation F(a, b) = v. By considering a small, circular restriction around the origin in n+1 dimensional space, a topological structure known as the Milnor fibration can be defined. By parameterizing this restriction using a unit vector a and a radius r, we obtain a map whose image, combined with a unit circle, parameterizes the boundary of a small, circular disc around v. This gives rise to a fibration over the circle whose fibers are diffeomorphic to the n+1 dimensional ball. However, considering all vectors a, these fibers can give rise to a space of polynomials whose arrangement can be analyzed. The study focuses on the effects of varying a, including the dimensions and monodromy characteristics of a specific subset of the fibers.

This research introduces an open-source, cross-platform data structure in A* that facilitates seamless integration between C# and Python libraries, maintaining compatibility with NumPy's multidimensional array format.

During the 17th century, scientists, particularly Galileo, heavily relied on observation and experimentation to uncover the underlying principles of science, but this focus led to a diminished understanding of the intricate details of how that knowledge is acquired. This critique, initially raised by Kant, is further explored by examining the case of Galileo's inclined plane experiments, illustrating the limitations of simply observing and conducting basic trials to deduce the principles of acceleration. Similar issues arise in more sophisticated studies, such as those performed by neurophysicists on cat visual cortex cells, highlighting the necessity of combining empirical evidence with theoretical analysis and a thorough examination of experimental procedures. This enhanced approach is essential to fully grasp the scientific principles at play and is particularly crucial in the age of advanced, automated experimentation, where the separation of principle-discovery and principle-testing is often blurred.

A comprehensive theory of q-Gaussian distributions is established, with a structured framework, including key concepts, relationships between subconcepts, and the capacity to model complex systems. Our research demonstrates that the binding q-energy derived from q-Gaussian statistics is a generalized form of traditional binding energy, with reduced values indicating deviations from classical behavior. A hierarchical hierarchy of families exists within our structured framework, with distinct characteristics. A sophisticated statistical approach is used to analyze and compare different families, with applications such as the examination of the Fermi q-Gaussian and Sato's families, which exhibit non-integer binding q-energy values. A non-Gaussian generalization of the Boltzmann entropy is introduced, with corresponding temperature definitions, including both the standard and Kaniadakis temperatures. Our work also includes an analysis of the high-energy behavior of these two distributions, which is expressed in terms of their respective q-values.

This study examines the outcome of magnetic island coalescence when a secondary current is applied, exploring how the island's behavior responds to various factors such as the location of the island, its size, and the polarity of the injected current. Utilizing a multidisciplinary approach that combines elements of magnetohydrodynamics and the dynamics of particle distributions, we observe that an appropriately sized and directed current can cause the island to stabilize and transition into a stationary state, independent of its initial characteristics. Conversely, an improperly oriented current may lead to the island's rapid collapse, resulting in the formation of a current sheet with unique distribution functions that cannot be derived from its predecessor's state. These findings have significant implications for magnetic reconnection processes, where understanding the island's dynamics is crucial.

Digital assistants on digital platforms learn to interact effectively with humans by observing, inferring, and adapting to their partners' cognitive strategies, much like evolutionary processes. This is particularly evident in collaborative online environments, where mutual adjustments take place. As a result, both the assistants and their human partners evolve cognitive abilities, such as heuristics and instincts, which improve their coordination. I will discuss three examples of cognitive co-evolution in online interactions, including digital trading platforms, cryptocurrency markets, and AI-powered poker games. I will highlight how these systems develop advanced problem-solving capabilities, such as solving complex Go puzzles within minutes, and provide insights into the benefits and ethical implications of cognitive load testing.
